claim: The African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri) is a naturally short-lived vertebrate.
source: Here, using the African turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri), a naturally short-lived vertebrate, we show that the gut microbiota plays a key role in modulating vertebrate life span.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction of the manuscript.

claim: Recolonizing the gut of middle-age killifish with bacteria from young donors resulted in life span extension.
source: Recolonizing the gut of middle-age individuals with bacteria from young donors resulted in life span extension and delayed behavioral decline.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data presented in Figure 4B showing that Ymt fish had significantly longer median life span compared to control groups.

claim: Recolonizing the gut of middle-age killifish with bacteria from young donors delayed behavioral decline.
source: Recolonizing the gut of middle-age individuals with bacteria from young donors resulted in life span extension and delayed behavioral decline.
evidence: This is supported by exploratory behavior data in Figure 4C showing that Ymt fish were more active at 16 weeks than control groups.

claim: Young gut microbiota transfer prevented the decrease in microbial diversity associated with host aging.
source: This intervention prevented the decrease in microbial diversity associated with host aging and maintained a young-like gut bacterial community, characterized by overrepresentation of the key genera Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Propionigenium and Psychrobacter.
evidence: This is supported by alpha diversity analysis in Figure 5A showing that Ymt fish had significantly higher bacterial richness at 16 weeks compared to wild-type controls.

claim: Young gut microbiota transfer maintained a young-like gut bacterial community characterized by overrepresentation of Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Propionigenium and Psychrobacter.
source: This intervention prevented the decrease in microbial diversity associated with host aging and maintained a young-like gut bacterial community, characterized by overrepresentation of the key genera Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Propionigenium and Psychrobacter.
evidence: This is supported by the cladogram in Figure 5D and boxplots in Figure 5E showing enrichment of these genera in young and Ymt fish.

claim: The insulin-IGF1 pathway regulates aging and life span across several species from yeast to mammals.
source: Genetic manipulations in model organisms have revealed key conserved molecular pathways, including the insulin-IGF1 and the mTOR pathways, which regulate aging and life span across several species, spanning from yeast to mammals (Kapahi et al., 2010; Kenyon et al., 1993; Lapierre and Hansen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The mTOR pathway regulates aging and life span across several species from yeast to mammals.
source: Genetic manipulations in model organisms have revealed key conserved molecular pathways, including the insulin-IGF1 and the mTOR pathways, which regulate aging and life span across several species, spanning from yeast to mammals (Kapahi et al., 2010; Kenyon et al., 1993; Lapierre and Hansen, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Lower temperatures have been associated with prolonged life span in several species.
source: Among these, lower temperatures (Conti et al., 2006; Miquel et al., 1976; Valenzano et al., 2006a; Van Voorhies and Ward, 1999) and reduced nutrient intake (Fontana et al., 2010; Mair and Dillin, 2008) are key environmental factors that have been associated with prolonged life span.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Reduced nutrient intake has been associated with prolonged life span.
source: Among these, lower temperatures (Conti et al., 2006; Miquel et al., 1976; Valenzano et al., 2006a; Van Voorhies and Ward, 1999) and reduced nutrient intake (Fontana et al., 2010; Mair and Dillin, 2008) are key environmental factors that have been associated with prolonged life span.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Gut microbial communities participate in nutrient absorption.
source: These microbial communities participate in a wide range of key biological processes, including nutrient absorption (Semova et al., 2012), development (Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013), metabolism (Nicholson et al., 2012), immune modulation (Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2017), defense against pathogens (Kamada et al., 2013; Schuijt et al., 2016) and disease (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gut microbial communities participate in development.
source: These microbial communities participate in a wide range of key biological processes, including nutrient absorption (Semova et al., 2012), development (Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013), metabolism (Nicholson et al., 2012), immune modulation (Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2017), defense against pathogens (Kamada et al., 2013; Schuijt et al., 2016) and disease (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gut microbial communities participate in metabolism.
source: These microbial communities participate in a wide range of key biological processes, including nutrient absorption (Semova et al., 2012), development (Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013), metabolism (Nicholson et al., 2012), immune modulation (Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2017), defense against pathogens (Kamada et al., 2013; Schuijt et al., 2016) and disease (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gut microbial communities participate in immune modulation.
source: These microbial communities participate in a wide range of key biological processes, including nutrient absorption (Semova et al., 2012), development (Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013), metabolism (Nicholson et al., 2012), immune modulation (Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2017), defense against pathogens (Kamada et al., 2013; Schuijt et al., 2016) and disease (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Gut microbial communities participate in defense against pathogens.
source: These microbial communities participate in a wide range of key biological processes, including nutrient absorption (Semova et al., 2012), development (Sommer and Bäckhed, 2013), metabolism (Nicholson et al., 2012), immune modulation (Geva-Zatorsky et al., 2017), defense against pathogens (Kamada et al., 2013; Schuijt et al., 2016) and disease (Sampson et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Individual gut microbiota composition changes dramatically during aging in flies, mice and humans.
source: Individual gut microbiota (GM) composition changes dramatically in various diseases (Baumgart and Carding, 2007; Garrett, 2015; Sokol et al., 2008) and during aging in flies, mice and humans (Clark et al., 2015; Langille et al., 2014; O'Toole and Jeffery, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Healthy gut microbiota is typically characterized by large bacterial taxonomic diversity.
source: Healthy GM is typically characterized by large bacterial taxonomic diversity, whereas frailty is associated with loss of diversity and expansion of more pathogenic bacterial species (Claesson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Frailty is associated with loss of gut microbial diversity and expansion of more pathogenic bacterial species.
source: Healthy GM is typically characterized by large bacterial taxonomic diversity, whereas frailty is associated with loss of diversity and expansion of more pathogenic bacterial species (Claesson et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Exceptionally long-lived individuals including supercentenarians are characterized by the persistence of bacterial taxa associated with a more healthy status.
source: Studies across different human age cohorts have shown that large changes in the abundance of subdominant bacterial taxa in the gut are a hallmark of aging; moreover, exceptionally long-lived individuals – including supercentenarians – are characterized by the persistence of bacterial taxa associated with a more healthy status (Biagi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Reducing gut microbiota dysbiosis by improving immune homeostasis promotes longer life span in flies.
source: In flies, reducing GM dysbiosis by improving immune homeostasis promotes longer life span (Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The turquoise killifish has a life span of a few months in captivity.
source: In this study, we develop the turquoise killifish (Nothobranchius furzeri), a naturally short-lived vertebrate species with a life span of a few months in captivity (Valenzano et al., 2015), as a new model organism to study aging in the host gut and microbiota.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Turquoise killifish have a complex gut microbiota both in the wild and in captivity.
source: We show that turquoise killifish (TK) have a complex GM (both in the wild and in captivity), similar in taxonomic diversity to that of mammals.
evidence: This claim is supported by 16S rRNA gene sequencing data from both wild and captive fish presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: During aging, the overall microbial diversity in the turquoise killifish gut decreases.
source: We also show that during aging the overall microbial diversity in the TK gut decreases, with increased over-representation of pathogenic Proteobacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha diversity analysis in Figure 3B showing decreased observed OTUs in old fish compared to young fish.

claim: During aging in turquoise killifish, there is increased over-representation of pathogenic Proteobacteria.
source: We also show that during aging the overall microbial diversity in the TK gut decreases, with increased over-representation of pathogenic Proteobacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cladogram in Figure 3D showing enrichment of Proteobacteria in old fish.

claim: Gut aging in turquoise killifish is associated with increased inflammation.
source: Transcriptome analysis additionally revealed that gut aging is associated with increased inflammation and reduced proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 3G showing enrichment of inflammatory response GO terms in old fish.

claim: Gut aging in turquoise killifish is associated with reduced proliferation.
source: Transcriptome analysis additionally revealed that gut aging is associated with increased inflammation and reduced proliferation.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data in Figure 3G showing enrichment of cell cycle and proliferation GO terms in young fish.

claim: The turquoise killifish genome sequence has become available.
source: The TK is a naturally short-lived vertebrate, whose genome sequence has become available (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015) and that is amenable to genetic manipulations via transgenesis or genome editing (Harel et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The turquoise killifish is amenable to genetic manipulations via transgenesis or genome editing.
source: The TK is a naturally short-lived vertebrate, whose genome sequence has become available (Reichwald et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2015) and that is amenable to genetic manipulations via transgenesis or genome editing (Harel et al., 2015; Valenzano et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The turquoise killifish is characterized by a broad spectrum of aging phenotypes including cancer, neurodegeneration, and behavioral decline.
source: Remarkably, this species is characterized by a broad spectrum of aging phenotypes, including cancer, neurodegeneration, and behavioral decline (Harel and Brunet, 2015; Kim et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Turquoise killifish are adapted to living in conditions of intermittent availability of water.
source: TK are adapted to living in conditions of intermittent availability of water and to surviving during brief rainy seasons and long dry seasons (Cellerino et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: In captivity, turquoise killifish live between four to eight months, depending on the strain.
source: In captivity, it lives between four to eight months, depending on the strain (Valenzano et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Turquoise killifish are characterized by a gut microbial taxonomic diversity similar to other longer-lived vertebrates including zebrafish, mice and humans.
source: We found that TK are characterized by a gut microbial taxonomic diversity similar to other, longer-lived vertebrates, including zebrafish, mice and humans (Kostic et al., 2013; Qin et al., 2010; Stephens et al., 2016) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis of bacterial diversity shown in Figure 1A and citations to published literature.

claim: Turquoise killifish gut bacterial taxonomic diversity is an order of magnitude higher than the gut microbial diversity present in invertebrate model organisms such as worms and flies in the laboratory.
source: This bacterial taxonomic diversity is an order of magnitude higher than the gut microbial diversity present in invertebrate model organisms such as worms (Cabreiro and Gems, 2013) and flies (Buchon et al., 2013) in the laboratory (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparative analysis shown in Figure 1A and citations to published literature.

claim: The four most abundant bacterial phyla in the turquoise killifish gut are Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes.
source: Remarkably, the four most abundant bacterial phyla present in the TK's gut, i.e. Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes, are also the four most abundant human gut bacterial divisions (Zoetendal et al., 2006) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1 and 2), although in different proportions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heatmap in Figure 1B showing phylum-level composition.

claim: The four most abundant bacterial phyla in the turquoise killifish gut are also the four most abundant human gut bacterial divisions.
source: Remarkably, the four most abundant bacterial phyla present in the TK's gut, i.e. Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes, are also the four most abundant human gut bacterial divisions (Zoetendal et al., 2006) (Figure 1B and Figure 1—source data 1 and 2), although in different proportions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the heatmap in Figure 1B and a citation to published literature.

claim: Proteobacteria was the dominant phylum in most wild turquoise killifish populations, similar to laboratory fish.
source: Sequencing these wild populations confirmed that Proteobacteria was the dominant phylum also in most wild populations, similar to laboratory fish (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the relative abundance data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Individuals from all wild turquoise killifish populations had a more diverse gut microbiota than laboratory fish.
source: Individuals from all wild populations had a more diverse GM than laboratory fish (Figure 2C, Shannon alpha diversity, Dunn Kruskal-Wallis test, BH-adjusted p values < 0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by Shannon diversity analysis shown in Figure 2C with statistical testing.

claim: Laboratory turquoise killifish share a core microbiota with wild populations.
source: Based on this, laboratory fish share a core microbiota with wild populations, despite the differences in culturing conditions between the laboratory and the wild, similar to what is seen in zebrafish (Roeselers et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by beta diversity analysis in Figure 2D-F showing that laboratory fish are contained within the natural variation of wild populations, and by citation to published literature on zebrafish.

claim: Bacterial taxonomic diversity significantly decreased between 6-week-old and 16-week-old turquoise killifish.
source: We found that bacterial taxonomic diversity (alpha diversity) significantly decreased between 6-week-old and 16-week-old fish, while bacterial abundance measured from stool was not changed (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha diversity analysis in Figure 3B showing significantly lower observed OTUs in old fish.

claim: Bacterial abundance measured from stool was not changed between 6-week-old and 16-week-old turquoise killifish.
source: We found that bacterial taxonomic diversity (alpha diversity) significantly decreased between 6-week-old and 16-week-old fish, while bacterial abundance measured from stool was not changed (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bacterial load data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Aging in the turquoise killifish is characterized by a significant reduction in gut bacterial richness, similar to humans.
source: This indicates that, similar to humans (Claesson et al., 2012), aging in the TK is characterized by a significant reduction in gut bacterial richness.
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha diversity data in Figure 3B and a citation to published literature on human aging.

claim: Bacterial composition was significantly altered between young and old turquoise killifish guts.
source: Bacterial composition was also significantly altered between young and old fish guts (Figure 3C), including an age-dependent decrease in Firmicutes (Kruskal-Wallis test, p value = 0.002) and Actinobacteria (Kruskal-Wallis test, p value = 0.013).
evidence: This claim is supported by beta diversity analysis in Figure 3C showing significant separation between young and old fish.

claim: There is an age-dependent decrease in Firmicutes in turquoise killifish guts.
source: Bacterial composition was also significantly altered between young and old fish guts (Figure 3C), including an age-dependent decrease in Firmicutes (Kruskal-Wallis test, p value = 0.002) and Actinobacteria (Kruskal-Wallis test, p value = 0.013).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of phylum-level abundance with p value = 0.002.

claim: There is an age-dependent decrease in Actinobacteria in turquoise killifish guts.
source: Bacterial composition was also significantly altered between young and old fish guts (Figure 3C), including an age-dependent decrease in Firmicutes (Kruskal-Wallis test, p value = 0.002) and Actinobacteria (Kruskal-Wallis test, p value = 0.013).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of phylum-level abundance with p value = 0.013.

claim: Young turquoise killifish guts were significantly enriched for Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes and Actinobacteria.
source: While young fish guts were significantly enriched for Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, old fish were dominated by Proteobacteria (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cladogram in Figure 3D showing enrichment of these phyla in young fish.

claim: Old turquoise killifish were dominated by Proteobacteria.
source: While young fish guts were significantly enriched for Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes and Actinobacteria, old fish were dominated by Proteobacteria (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cladogram in Figure 3D showing enrichment of Proteobacteria in old fish.

claim: Young turquoise killifish had gut microbiota associated with glycolysis and polysaccharide metabolism.
source: While young fish had GM associated with glycolysis and polysaccharide metabolism, old fish's GM was depleted of bacteria associated with carbohydrate, nucleotide and amino acid metabolism, and was enriched for bacteria associated with pathogenesis, transport and catabolism (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by predicted metagenome function analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Old turquoise killifish gut microbiota was depleted of bacteria associated with carbohydrate, nucleotide and amino acid metabolism.
source: While young fish had GM associated with glycolysis and polysaccharide metabolism, old fish's GM was depleted of bacteria associated with carbohydrate, nucleotide and amino acid metabolism, and was enriched for bacteria associated with pathogenesis, transport and catabolism (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by predicted metagenome function analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Old turquoise killifish gut microbiota was enriched for bacteria associated with pathogenesis, transport and catabolism.
source: While young fish had GM associated with glycolysis and polysaccharide metabolism, old fish's GM was depleted of bacteria associated with carbohydrate, nucleotide and amino acid metabolism, and was enriched for bacteria associated with pathogenesis, transport and catabolism (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by predicted metagenome function analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Bacterial motility and flagellar assembly was strongly increased in gut microbiota from old turquoise killifish.
source: In particular, bacterial motility and flagellar assembly was strongly increased in GM from old fish.
evidence: This claim is supported by predicted metagenome function analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Bacterial motility and flagellar assembly are associated with increased virulence in bacteria.
source: These terms are associated with increased virulence in bacteria (Josenhans and Suerbaum, 2002), supporting that old fish had a higher prevalence of potentially pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Young turquoise killifish had a distinct expression signature of active proliferation.
source: Young fish had a distinct expression signature of active proliferation (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with the bacterial metagenomic signature of replication.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Old turquoise killifish had significant Gene Ontology terms associated with immune and defense responses against pathogens as well as inflammation.
source: Old fish, on the other hand, had significant Gene Ontology terms associated with immune and defense responses against pathogens as well as inflammation, consistent with the bacterial metagenome signatures associated with host disease and overall virulence.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-Seq data and GO term analysis shown in Figure 3G and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Antibiotic treatment significantly reduced gut microbial content compared to pre-treatment levels in turquoise killifish.
source: The antibiotic treatment significantly reduced gut microbial content compared to pre-treatment levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by bacterial load quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fish receiving young gut microbiota transfer (Ymt) underwent dramatic life span prolongation compared to antibiotic-only treated fish (Abx) with 21% increase in median life span.
source: Ymt fish underwent dramatic life span prolongation compared to three control groups, which received: (i) antibiotic-only (Abx) (21% life span increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 5.89E-05), (ii) antibiotics and same-age (i.e. 9.5 weeks) gut content (Omt) (41% increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 5.08E-06), or (iii) no-treatment (wt) (37% increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 4.04E-09) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4B with statistical testing.

claim: Fish receiving young gut microbiota transfer (Ymt) underwent dramatic life span prolongation compared to fish receiving same-age gut content (Omt) with 41% increase in median life span.
source: Ymt fish underwent dramatic life span prolongation compared to three control groups, which received: (i) antibiotic-only (Abx) (21% life span increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 5.89E-05), (ii) antibiotics and same-age (i.e. 9.5 weeks) gut content (Omt) (41% increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 5.08E-06), or (iii) no-treatment (wt) (37% increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 4.04E-09) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4B with statistical testing.

claim: Fish receiving young gut microbiota transfer (Ymt) underwent dramatic life span prolongation compared to no-treatment controls (wt) with 37% increase in median life span.
source: Ymt fish underwent dramatic life span prolongation compared to three control groups, which received: (i) antibiotic-only (Abx) (21% life span increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 5.89E-05), (ii) antibiotics and same-age (i.e. 9.5 weeks) gut content (Omt) (41% increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 5.08E-06), or (iii) no-treatment (wt) (37% increase in median life span, Logrank test p value = 4.04E-09) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4B with statistical testing.

claim: Acute antibiotic treatment alone was sufficient to increase turquoise killifish life span compared to the wild-type group with 14% median life span increase.
source: Noteworthy, acute antibiotic treatment alone was sufficient to increase fish life span compared to the wt group (14% median life span increase, Logrank test p value = 0.0129) (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4B with statistical testing.

claim: Fish receiving same-age gut microbiota transfer (Omt) did not live longer than the control, wild-type group.
source: However, Omt fish did not live longer than the control, wt group (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Spontaneous exploratory behavior in turquoise killifish decreases with age.
source: It was shown in previous work that spontaneous exploratory behavior in TK decreases with age (Genade et al., 2005; Valenzano et al., 2006b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Young 6-week-old turquoise killifish were significantly more active than 16-week-old fish.
source: Young, 6-week-old fish, were significantly more active than 16-week-old fish (Figure 4—source data 3 and Figure 4C, Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 10.752, df = 1, p value = 0.00104).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 4C with statistical testing.

claim: Fish receiving young gut microbiota transfer (Ymt) were more active at 16 weeks of life than fish receiving same-age gut content (Omt) and wild-type fish at the same age.
source: Remarkably, Ymt were more active at 16 weeks of life than Omt and wt fish at the same age, resembling younger fish performance (Figure 4C, Dunn Kruskal-Wallis multiple comparison test, BH-adjusted p value = 0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by locomotor activity data shown in Figure 4C with statistical testing.

claim: At one week post transfer, there were no significant differences in alpha diversity metrics among treatment groups.
source: One week post transfer there were no significant differences in alpha diversity metrics among treatment groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha diversity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: At one-week post transfer, Ymt and Omt fish had significantly different gut microbial population diversity.
source: However, at one-week post transfer, Ymt and Omt fish had already significantly different gut microbial population diversity (Unweighted UniFrac and Bray-Curtis distances, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by beta diversity analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: Seven weeks after microbial transfer, Ymt fish had significantly higher bacterial richness compared to wild-type 16-week-old fish.
source: Seven weeks after the microbial transfer (16 weeks of age, corresponding to the median life span for this species in captivity), Ymt fish had significantly higher bacterial richness compared to wild-type, 16-week-old fish (Figure 5A, Dunn Kruskal-Wallis test, BH-adjusted p value = 0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha diversity analysis shown in Figure 5A with statistical testing.

claim: One acute gut microbiota transfer had long-lasting effects on gut microbiota diversity in turquoise killifish.
source: This shows that one acute transfer had long-lasting effects on GM diversity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that Ymt fish maintained higher bacterial richness at 16 weeks (7 weeks post-transfer) as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gut microbiota community structure in Ymt fish was significantly altered compared to Omt and 16-week-old wild-type fish.
source: GM community structure in Ymt fish was also significantly altered compared to Omt and 16wk (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E); however, it did not statistically differ from young wild-type fish, i.e. the 6wk group.
evidence: This claim is supported by beta diversity analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Gut microbiota community structure in Ymt fish did not statistically differ from young wild-type fish.
source: GM community structure in Ymt fish was also significantly altered compared to Omt and 16wk (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E); however, it did not statistically differ from young wild-type fish, i.e. the 6wk group.
evidence: This claim is supported by beta diversity analysis shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Based on hierarchical clustering, Ymt fish clustered preferentially with 6-week-old fish.
source: Furthermore, based on hierarchical clustering, Ymt fish clustered preferentially with 6wk fish (Figure 5C), showing that the GM-transfer from young donors significantly reset a young-like GM.
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Young fish and fish treated with young gut microbiota were more enriched with members of the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes.
source: Young fish (6wk), as well as fish treated with young GM (Ymt), were more enriched with members of the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes (Figure 5D) and with the genera Carnobacterium, Arthrobacter, Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Psychrobacter, Enterococcus and Halomonas (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cladogram in Figure 5D showing enrichment of these phyla.

claim: Young fish and fish treated with young gut microbiota were enriched with the genera Carnobacterium, Arthrobacter, Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Psychrobacter, Enterococcus and Halomonas.
source: Young fish (6wk), as well as fish treated with young GM (Ymt), were more enriched with members of the Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes (Figure 5D) and with the genera Carnobacterium, Arthrobacter, Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Psychrobacter, Enterococcus and Halomonas (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by boxplots in Figure 5E showing relative abundance of these genera.

claim: Proteobacteria had higher connectivity in the shorter-lived 16-week-old and Omt groups compared to 6-week-old, Ymt and Abx groups.
source: Using this analysis, we found that Proteobacteria had higher connectivity in the shorter-lived 16wk and Omt groups compared to 6wk, Ymt and Abx (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-occurrence network analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 6-week-old and Ymt fish had the largest bacterial co-occurrence networks and a higher number of highly-connected nodes (hub nodes).
source: Overall, 6wk and Ymt fish had the largest networks and a higher number of highly-connected nodes (hub nodes), showing that a few genera of bacteria significantly co-occurred with a large set of other bacterial genera (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: Young mice gut microbiota had more significantly connected nodes and a higher number of bacterial hubs compared to middle-age and old mice.
source: Similar to what we found in TK, young mice GM had more significantly connected nodes and a higher number of bacterial hubs compared to middle-age and old mice (Figure 6B, inset).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of published mouse data shown in Figure 6B inset.

claim: One hub bacterial cluster in Ymt fish was composed of bacterial genera that were also hub-bacteria in young wild-type fish and included Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Propionigenium and Psychrobacter.
source: Strikingly, one was composed of bacterial genera that were also hub-bacteria in young wild-type fish (6wk) and included Exiguobacterium, Planococcus, Propionigenium and Psychrobacter (Figure 6C, Ymt network, green nodes), while the other was composed of hub bacteria from old wild-type fish (16wk) hub and included Propionibacterium, Delftia, and Citrobacter (Figure 6C and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The bacterial hubs identified in Omt and Abx overlapped exclusively with the old wild-type group.
source: Remarkably, the bacterial hubs identified in Omt and Abx overlapped exclusively with the old wild-type group (16wk) (Figure 6C, orange nodes, and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Bacterial network topology reflects host age both in fish and mice, with younger biological age associated with larger networks.
source: These results support that bacterial network topology reflects host age both in fish and mice, with younger biological age associated with larger networks.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the network analyses shown in Figure 6B and C comparing young and old fish and mice.

claim: Host gene transcripts separated based on fish age, and all the transcriptomes obtained from 16 week old fish groups clustered together.
source: Interestingly, while young GM transfer reset a young-like GM environment in aged fish, host gene transcripts separated based on fish age, and all the transcriptomes obtained from 16 week old fish groups (16wk, Omt, Ymt) clustered together (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is supported by cluster analysis of RNA-Seq data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Comparing transcriptomes in Omt and Ymt revealed a distinct signature of defense response to bacteria in Ymt.
source: However, comparing transcriptomes in Omt and Ymt revealed a distinct signature of defense response to bacteria in Ymt and increased expression of genes associated with hyaluronic acid metabolism in Omt (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term enrichment shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Comparing transcriptomes in Omt and Ymt revealed increased expression of genes associated with hyaluronic acid metabolism in Omt.
source: However, comparing transcriptomes in Omt and Ymt revealed a distinct signature of defense response to bacteria in Ymt and increased expression of genes associated with hyaluronic acid metabolism in Omt (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis and GO term enrichment shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Genes associated with the TOR-pathway (DEPTOR) and with cell adhesion and extracellular matrix composition (DSCAM) were significantly changed comparing 16-week-old and Omt with 6-week-old fish, but unchanged between Ymt and 6-week-old fish.
source: Comparing the expression levels of all groups to the 6wk group, we identified a set of genes whose expression in the gut was significantly changed comparing 16wk and Omt with 6wk; comparing 16wk and Ymt, but unchanged between Ymt and 6wk (Fisher exact test, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR = 0.1). These were genes associated with the TOR-pathway (DEPTOR) and with cell adhesion and extracellular matrix composition (DSCAM) (Figure 7D), suggesting a potential difference in cell adhesion and gut permeability between 16wk and Omt from one side, and Ymt and 6wk on the other side.
evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 7D with statistical testing.

claim: Hub genera shared between Ymt and young fish networks are highly correlated with transcripts including Jak2 and several genes encoding ribosomal proteins.
source: Remarkably, these genes include Jak2, an important gene involved in cellular proliferation and differentiation, and several genes encoding S and L- ribosomal proteins (RPS and RPL genes) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), whose expression in other species has been strongly associated with aging and longevity (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by OTU-transcript correlation analysis shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2, and by citation to published literature.

claim: Expression of ribosomal protein genes in other species has been strongly associated with aging and longevity.
source: Remarkably, these genes include Jak2, an important gene involved in cellular proliferation and differentiation, and several genes encoding S and L- ribosomal proteins (RPS and RPL genes) (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), whose expression in other species has been strongly associated with aging and longevity (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Hyaluronic acid metabolism has been associated with increased inflammation, deregulated immune response and risk for cancer.
source: Remarkably, hyaluronic acid metabolism, altered between the experimental groups receiving young and old gut contents, has been associated with increased inflammation, deregulated immune response and risk for cancer (Cho et al., 2017; Tian et al., 2013), all of which could provide the basis for life span modulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Laboratory-raised turquoise killifish are dominated by a few high-abundance bacterial taxa that are already present in wild killifish populations.
source: Laboratory-raised fish are not represented by distinct gut bacterial communities, but are rather dominated by a few high-abundance bacterial taxa that are already present in wild killifish populations.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the beta diversity analysis in Figure 2D-F showing that laboratory fish are contained within the natural variation of wild populations.

claim: Wild populations of turquoise killifish show large between-population gut bacterial diversity, with the emergence of population-specific high-abundance taxa.
source: Additionally, we found that wild populations of TK show large between-population gut bacterial diversity, with the emergence of population-specific high-abundance taxa.
evidence: This claim is supported by beta diversity analysis in Figure 2E-F showing higher between-population diversity.

claim: While individual bacterial diversity (alpha diversity) is higher in young individuals, old fish are more dissimilar from one another.
source: Intriguingly, while individual bacterial diversity (alpha diversity) is higher in young individuals, old fish are more dissimilar from one another, that is, while each individual old fish has a more homogeneous GM composition than young fish, any two old individuals have more divergent bacterial communities compared to young individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha and beta diversity analyses in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: Aging in turquoise killifish was associated with reduced bacterial species richness and loss of bacterial taxonomic units involved in carbohydrate, nucleotide and amino acid metabolism.
source: Aging in this experimental model was not only associated with reduced bacterial species richness, but more specifically with loss of bacterial taxonomic units involved in carbohydrate, nucleotide and amino acid metabolism, which in mice are associated with aging (Langille et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by alpha diversity analysis in Figure 3B and predicted metagenome function analysis in Figure 3E, and by citation to published literature.

claim: The shift in microbial composition between young and old turquoise killifish was characterized by a higher prevalence of Proteobacteria in old individuals.
source: The shift in microbial composition between young and old fish was consistently characterized by a higher prevalence of Proteobacteria in old individuals, while young individuals were significantly more enriched in Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cladogram in Figure 3D showing phylum-level differences.

claim: Young individuals were significantly more enriched in Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes.
source: The shift in microbial composition between young and old fish was consistently characterized by a higher prevalence of Proteobacteria in old individuals, while young individuals were significantly more enriched in Firmicutes, Actinobacteria and Bacteroidetes.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cladogram in Figure 3D showing phylum-level differences.

claim: Young fish gut microbiota was associated with carbohydrate metabolism, replication and repair, as well as DNA repair.
source: Additionally, functional metagenome analysis showed that young fish had GM associated with carbohydrate metabolism, replication and repair, as well as DNA repair, indicating the young GM's ability to protect itself against assault and thus maintain homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by predicted metagenome function analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Bacterial pathogenicity in the gut is associated with the accumulation of mutations over time, induced by the failed capacity to repair them.
source: On the other hand, bacterial pathogenicity in the gut is associated with the accumulation of mutations over time, induced by the failed capacity to repair them (Leimbach et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Life span was not affected in young fish exposed to gut microbiota from old, young, and sham control fish after antibiotic treatment.
source: Additionally, life span was not affected in young fish exposed to GM from old, young, and sham control fish after antibiotic treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Young fish receiving 16-week-old gut microbiota content did not live significantly shorter than young control fish.
source: Since we observed that young fish receiving 16-week-old gut microbiota content did not live significantly shorter than young, control fish, it is plausible that dysbiosis, in the context of a young gut immune function, does not lead to increased mortality.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Species of Exiguobacterium and Propionigenium are able to metabolize cellulose and ferment carbohydrates to produce short chain fatty acids.
source: Specifically, species of Exiguobacterium and Propionigenium are able to metabolize cellulose and ferment carbohydrates to produce short chain fatty acids, which are known anti-inflammatory mediators and can modulate the immune system.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about these bacterial genera.

claim: Short chain fatty acids are known anti-inflammatory mediators and can modulate the immune system.
source: Specifically, species of Exiguobacterium and Propionigenium are able to metabolize cellulose and ferment carbohydrates to produce short chain fatty acids, which are known anti-inflammatory mediators and can modulate the immune system.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about short chain fatty acids.

claim: Planococcus species can hydrolyze gelatin to produce essential amino acids for use by the host.
source: Planococcus species can hydrolyze gelatin to produce essential amino acids for use by the host and certain Psychrobacter species are capable of producing omega-fatty acids.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Planococcus species.

claim: Certain Psychrobacter species are capable of producing omega-fatty acids.
source: Planococcus species can hydrolyze gelatin to produce essential amino acids for use by the host and certain Psychrobacter species are capable of producing omega-fatty acids.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about Psychrobacter species.

claim: Young gut microbiota could lead to beneficial effects on host survival and behavior performance both via delayed dysbiosis and direct favorable effects of subsets of young microbes.
source: Therefore, young GM could possibly lead to beneficial effects on host survival and behavior performance both via delayed dysbiosis and direct favorable effects of subsets of young microbes.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that Ymt fish live longer than Abx fish and have better locomotor performance.

claim: The turquoise killifish is the shortest-lived vertebrate to date reproduced in captivity.
source: Since it is the shortest-lived vertebrate to date reproduced in captivity, the TK can become an ideal model to dissect the links between GM diversity and host aging.
evidence: This claim is based on knowledge of vertebrate life spans in captivity.

claim: Middle-age gut microbiota composition might be primed to induce damage in the host.
source: Since Abx outlived Omt and wild-type fish, while Ymt fish outlived Abx fish, it is plausible that middle-age GM composition might be primed to induce damage in the host and that its removal is therefore beneficial.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the survival data showing that antibiotic treatment alone extends life span.

claim: Young gut microbiota has beneficial effects on host physiology that are additive to the effects of antibiotic treatment.
source: However, as the recolonization of middle-age individuals with young fish gut content after antibiotic treatment prolongs life span even more, this implies that young GM, per se, has beneficial effects on host physiology that are additive to the effects of the antibiotic treatment.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the survival data showing that Ymt fish live longer than Abx fish.

claim: The timing of gut microbiota transfer is critical to inducing systemic effects and modulating life span.
source: These results suggest that the timing of GM transfer is critical to inducing systemic effects and modulating life span.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that GM transfer to young fish did not affect life span, while transfer to middle-age fish did.

claim: The age-associated decline of immune function might be responsible for the progressively decreased capacity of the host to maintain the healthy portion of the gut microbiota community.
source: These results are compatible with a scenario where the age-associated decline of immune function might be responsible for the progressively decreased capacity of the host to (i) maintain the healthy portion of the GM community and (ii) counteract the proliferation of potentially pathogenic gut bacteria.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that young fish receiving old GM did not have reduced life span.

claim: The age-associated decline of immune function might be responsible for the progressively decreased capacity of the host to counteract the proliferation of potentially pathogenic gut bacteria.
source: These results are compatible with a scenario where the age-associated decline of immune function might be responsible for the progressively decreased capacity of the host to (i) maintain the healthy portion of the GM community and (ii) counteract the proliferation of potentially pathogenic gut bacteria.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the observation that young fish receiving old GM did not have reduced life span.

claim: Dysbiosis, in the context of a young gut immune function, does not lead to increased mortality.
source: Since we observed that young fish receiving 16-week-old gut microbiota content did not live significantly shorter than young, control fish, it is plausible that dysbiosis, in the context of a young gut immune function, does not lead to increased mortality.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the survival data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Enhanced defense response against bacteria in Ymt compared to Omt is compatible with an increased capacity to resist the attack of pathogenic gut bacteria.
source: However, enhanced defense response against bacteria in Ymt compared to Omt is compatible with an increased capacity to resist to the attack of pathogenic gut bacteria, which could provide the basis for longer life span.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the differential gene expression analysis in Figure 7B-C.

claim: Transfer of young gut microbiota to middle-age individuals might be affecting host gut proliferation and differentiation, as well as ribosomal biogenesis.
source: This resource suggests that transfer of young gut microbiota to middle-age individuals might be affecting host gut proliferation and differentiation, as well as ribosomal biogenesis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the OTU-transcript correlation analysis in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bacterial consortia associated with young fish can contribute to increased life span and enhanced individual health status.
source: Fish treated with young GM after depletion of their own resident GM community not only maintained a more diverse microbial community at old age compared to wild-type, age-matched control fish, but their microbial community remained more similar to that of young fish. This raises the possibility that bacterial consortia associated with young fish can contribute to increased life span and enhanced individual health status.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the observation that Ymt fish maintained young-like GM and lived longer.
